vision_features.image_context: Close-up view of a soybean plant in a field setting. Multiple plant organs are visible: stems, trifoliate leaves (both healthy green and severely affected), and seed pods. The background shows a field of predominantly dry, straw-colored plants at an advanced growth stage. A person in white clothing is partially visible at the right edge.
vision_features.abnormalities: 1. Severely wilted/collapsed leaves (lower-center and right of frame): Three leaflets of a trifoliate leaf are completely collapsed, shriveled, and curled inward. The tissue is dry, papery, and tan-to-light-brown in color. The texture is crinkled and brittle-looking, with the vein structure still visible but the tissue between veins appearing collapsed. The affected leaflets are medium-to-large in size (approximately 6–8 cm estimated). Some areas show darker brown, moist-looking patches, especially near the leaf attachment points, suggesting more recently dead tissue. The edges are ragged and curled. Distribution is confined to one full trifoliate unit hanging from a central petiole. 2. Dark discoloration on the stem: At the node where an affected trifoliate attaches, there is a small dark gray-to-black discoloration on the stem surface, approximately 5–10 mm in length, with no clearly defined border. The texture appears slightly sunken relative to the surrounding green stem tissue. 3. Partially dried pod nearby (upper left): One small pod visible near the upper-left area appears tan-brown and deflated, consistent with advanced drying; its surface is smooth and papery. 4. Small scattered tan spots on otherwise green leaflets: On one of the still-green trifoliate leaves (center), there are a few small (2–4 mm), roughly circular, pale tan to light brown dry spots scattered across the blade surface. These have no distinct visible border or halo and appear dry and flat.
vision_features.absences: 1. No powdery or dusty coating is visible on any leaf surface. 2. No raised pustules, tiny raised dots, or thread-like structures are visible within or on the dry collapsed leaf tissue. 3. No visible yellowing (pale green or yellow halo) surrounding the dry tan spots on the green leaves. 4. No visible slimy or wet exudate on the stem discoloration or collapsed leaf tissue.
vision_features.summary: The most severely affected organ is a trifoliate leaf whose three leaflets have completely collapsed, dried, and curled into a crinkled, papery tan-brown mass, still attached to the plant. A small dark gray-to-black patch is present on the stem at the attachment node of this affected trifoliate. The surrounding field is predominantly dry and straw-colored, indicating a late-season crop, while the focal plant retains some green leaves. The single most striking feature is the stark contrast between the fully collapsed, crinkled, dead-brown trifoliate and the adjacent still-living green leaves on the same plant.

trace.result_text:
Available classes in 'Soybean_Diseases' (3 total):
   1. Phyllosticta_leaf_spot
   2. Phytophthora
   3. Tobacco_Streak_Virus

Knowledge-base entry for 'Phyllosticta_leaf_spot':
────────────────────────────────────────
Lesions most often occur on leaves and are circular, oval, and irregular or V-shaped. Lesions appear gray or tan and have a narrow, dark margin. Irregularly shaped tan/brownish lesions with purplish margins may be observed in the lower canopy.. In older lesions, numerous small, black specks (i.e., pycnidia) may be visible.
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Phytophthora':
────────────────────────────────────────
Young plants show rapid yellowing and wilting with soft rot and collapse of the root. Mature plants exhibit general yellowing of lower leaves progressing upward, followed by wilting and death, with brown discolored roots and a dark chocolate-brown stem discoloration extending from below the soil line upward several nodes; leaves typically stay attached after plant death.. The best diagnostic symptom on susceptible varieties is a lower stem discoloration (dark chocolate-brown) that may extend several nodes up the stem. Root system shows lateral and branch roots almost completely discolored; tap roots with brown surface discoloration and tan to brown inner tissue discoloration. Leaves turn yellow, wilt, and typically stay attached after plant death.. stem canker, Pythium
────────────────────────────────────────

Knowledge-base entry for 'Tobacco_Streak_Virus':
────────────────────────────────────────
Symptoms include bud blight, shepherd's crooking, stunting, wilting, delayed maturity, bud and leaf proliferation, reduced pod number, discolored, distorted, and dead leaves, discoloration and dead streaks at nodes, dark spots on pods, and delayed seed development.. Pod lesions, proliferation of tissue, discoloration and dead streaks at nodes, dark spots on pods, and seed discoloration are characteristic features.
────────────────────────────────────────

DISCRIMINATING: 'Phytophthora' vs 'Tobacco_Streak_Virus'
Ruling feature : Dark chocolate-brown stem/root discoloration below the soil line vs. dead streaks at nodes with pod lesions and tissue proliferation
Phytophthora: Disease A (Phytophthora) shows a distinctive dark chocolate-brown discoloration of the lower stem extending from below the soil line upward several nodes, with brown discolored roots and leaves that remain attached after plant death.
Tobacco_Streak_Virus: Disease B (Tobacco Streak Virus) shows dead streaks and discoloration specifically at nodes, along with pod lesions, dark spots on pods, bud blight, shepherd's crooking, and proliferation of bud/leaf tissue — with no described root or lower-stem browning.
Decision rule  : IF the plant shows a dark chocolate-brown stem discoloration originating below the soil line and extending up several nodes with decayed roots and leaves remaining attached, THEN diagnose Phytophthora; IF the plant shows dead streaks at nodes, dark spots on pods, bud blight/shepherd's crooking, and tissue proliferation without lower-stem/root browning, THEN diagnose Tobacco Streak Virus.
